title: The Outreach Checklist: How Many Right-Fit People You Need for the Replies You Want
description: Reply rate isn't your problem. Your crowd is too small. Size your market, split it into segments, verify it and work out how many people you need.
lead: This is the full outreach checklist from the reel. You get the crowd-size math, a 6-step checklist for building an audience that is big enough and the right fit, a fill-in sheet you can paste into Google Sheets, a worked example, a problem finder and a prompt that sizes your market for you.
insider: Before we scale any client campaign, we size the crowd first: how many right-fit people exist, how many segments they split into, and how many we must reach for the replies the client wants. In one small pilot, **10,284 people contacted turned into 417 replies and 103 sales opportunities**, about 1 in every 100 people. The checklist is the easy part; the full system (list, inboxes, follow-ups) is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: The short answer

In the campaign in the reel, one client sent **84,643 emails** in one real month and got **2,399 replies**. About **1 in 28 people** replied. That sounds great until you flip it: if you only email 28 people, you should expect **one reply**. Maybe zero.

So when a small campaign gets no replies, the reply rate usually isn't the problem. **Your crowd is too small.** The fix is simple math: decide how many replies you want, then work out how many right-fit people you need to reach to get them.

The 3% column comes from [Hunter's State of Email Outreach 2026](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), which found sales outreach sequences get a **3% average reply rate**, counted per recipient. All numbers are rounded up, because you can't email part of a person.
Why 28 people tell you nothing
Each person has a small chance of replying. With small groups, luck decides the result, not your email. Even if your campaign truly gets 1 reply per 28 people, here's what chance alone does:

Read the first row again. **More than 1 time in 3, a campaign that works will show zero replies from 28 people.** Most people quit right there and rewrite a good email. With a few hundred people, zero replies almost never happens by luck. If you see it at that size, something is really wrong, and now you know it.

blocks.label: The math behind it
blocks.text: Chance of zero replies = (27 ÷ 28) to the power of the number of people. For 28 people: (27 ÷ 28)^28 ≈ 0.36, so about 36%.
Big crowd, small rooms

Wait, isn't smaller better? Hunter found that sequences sent to **21 to 50 people got a 6.2% reply rate, vs 2.4% for 500 or more**. But read Hunter's own takeaway: they are not telling you to stop at 50. They say to **cut your audience into smaller segments** and write copy that fits each one, then scale that.

So you need both. A **big total crowd**, so you have enough people to get real replies and real data. And **small rooms inside it**, so every email feels like it was written for that reader. A crowd of 5,000 is not one giant blast. It's 100 rooms of 50.
The outreach checklist
Six steps. Do them in order. Each one has the why and the how.
1. Write down who fits (and who doesn't)

**Why:** a big list of the wrong people is still the wrong people. Hunter's survey found **61% of decision makers** say cold emails fail because they aren't relevant. Fit rules keep your crowd big *and* right.

items: **Industry:** the 1 to 3 industries where your best customers come from.
**Company size:** a range of employees or revenue, not "any".
**Location:** the states, regions or countries you can actually serve.
**Role:** the job titles of the person who says yes (the buyer, not the user).
**A sign they need you now:** hiring, new location, new funding, bad reviews, running ads, and so on.
**The no list:** current clients, past clients who left, competitors, partners and anyone who asked you to stop.

blocks.text: 2. Count your whole crowd

**Why:** the total number of right-fit people tells you two things before you send a single email: whether your goal is possible, and how many months you can run before you email the same people again.

items: Put your fit rules into your lead database, LinkedIn search or Google Maps search. Write down the number of **companies** that match.
Pick how many people you'll contact per company. Hunter found that emailing **1 or 2 people per company** got a **5.1% reply rate, vs 3.5% for 3 or more**. Start with 1 or 2.
Total crowd = companies × people per company.
Expect to lose some to verification (step 5). Write down the crowd you can really reach.

blocks.text: 3. Work out how many people you need
**Why:** "send more emails" is not a plan. A number is. Working backwards from replies tells you exactly how big your crowd has to be each month.

items: **People to reach** = replies you want × people per reply. (At 1 in 28: 40 replies × 28 = 1,120 people)
**Raw contacts to pull** = people to reach ÷ the share that passes verification. (1,120 ÷ 0.8 = 1,400)
**Companies to find** = raw contacts ÷ people per company. (1,400 ÷ 2 = 700 companies)
**Months of runway** = reachable crowd ÷ people to reach per month.

blocks.label: Which reply rate to use
blocks.text: If you have your own numbers from at least a few hundred people, use them. If not, start with Hunter's 3% for sales and replace it after your first full month.
4. Split the crowd into small rooms

**Why:** Hunter's data says tight segments win, and [Instantly's 2026 benchmark report](https://instantly.ai/cold-email-benchmark-report-2026) names **micro-segmentation** as one of the biggest reasons top senders reach 10%+ reply rates while the average is **3.43%**.

items: Split by one thing at a time: industry first, then role or company size, then location or signal.
Give each segment its own first line and its own proof (a result from their world).
Aim for sending groups of about 50 people who have a lot in common. You can run many of them.
Name every segment clearly (for example: "Dental - owners - Texas - hiring") so you can compare results later.

blocks.text: 5. Verify before you send

**Why:** a crowd you can't reach doesn't count. Hunter found the **average bounce rate is 3.6%**, and Instantly says to keep bounces **under 2%**, because every bounce hurts your sender reputation. [Google's sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126) also tell senders to stop emailing addresses that bounce again and again.

items: Run every list through an email verifier before it goes into your sending tool.
Remove invalid emails. Be careful with **catch-all** addresses: Instantly warns they carry a higher bounce risk.
Remove duplicates and everyone on your no list.
Write down how many contacts survived. That's your real keep rate for the math in step 3.

blocks.text: 6. Let the whole sequence finish, then judge

**Why:** a person isn't done until they get every email in the sequence. Instantly found **58% of replies come from the first email and 42% from follow-ups**, and Hunter found **3 emails got 6.8% vs 3.3% for 1 email**. Judge too early and you miss almost half your replies.

items: Judge an angle (offer, first line, proof) only after **a few hundred people** finished the full sequence. Add up all the small rooms that used it.
Compare segments to each other, not to your hopes.
Keep what works, rewrite what doesn't, and send it to the next few hundred.

blocks.text: The fill-in sheet
Open a blank Google Sheet, click cell A1 and paste this. Labels land in column A, numbers and formulas in column B. Change the numbers in B1 to B5 to yours.

blocks.label: Copy, then paste into cell A1
blocks.text:
Replies you want per month	40
People per reply (1 in ...)	28
Share that passes verification	80%
People per company	2
Companies that fit (total)	6000
	
People to reach per month	=B1*B2
Raw contacts to pull per month	=ROUNDUP(B7/B3,0)
Companies to find per month	=ROUNDUP(B8/B4,0)
Reachable people in your whole market	=B5*B4*B3
Months before you run out	=ROUND(B10/B7,1)
Worked example
An IT services company wants **40 replies a month** from office managers and owners at small firms. These are example numbers to show the math, so swap in your own.

Now the rooms. The 6,000 companies split into 3 industries × 2 size bands = **6 segments of about 1,000 companies**. Each month the company pulls about **117 companies from each segment** (700 ÷ 6 ≈ 117) and sends them in groups of about 50 with copy written for that group.
Compare that with the room of 28. Email 28 people and you expect 1 reply, with a 36% chance of none. Email 1,120 people with the same email and you expect about 40, and a bad week can't fool you.

blocks.label: If your runway is short
blocks.text: Under 3 months of runway means your fit rules are too tight for the goal. Add a nearby industry, a second buyer role or a new region, and size it again before you send.
Problem finder: is it the crowd or the message?

head: What you see
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Keep going until a few hundred people finish the sequence
Wrong fit, wrong offer, or emails landing in spam
Check the fit rules first, then test inbox placement, then rewrite
Replies, but mostly "not interested" or "wrong person"
Crowd is big but not the right fit
Tighten the role and the "need you now" sign
One segment replies, another is silent
The silent segment needs different copy or isn't a fit
Give it its own first line and proof, or drop it
List not verified, or too old
Ran out of people in 3 weeks
Total market smaller than your monthly need
Widen the fit rules or lower the monthly goal

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Judging a campaign on 20 to 50 people.** Luck runs the result at that size.
**Fixing the small crowd with a bad list.** More of the wrong people only adds noise and spam complaints.
**One giant blast.** A big crowd needs many small rooms, each with its own copy.
**Emailing 4 people at every company.** Hunter's data favors 1 or 2.
**Skipping verification to save time.** Bounces burn the inboxes you need for the whole crowd.
**Calling it after email 1.** About 4 in 10 replies come from follow-ups.

blocks.text: Size your crowd with Claude

blocks.label: Crowd size prompt
blocks.text:
Act as my cold email list planner.

What I sell: [one sentence]
My best customers: [industry, company size, location, buyer job title]
Replies I want per month: [number]
My reply rate per person: [use 3% if I don't know]
People I'll contact per company: [1 or 2]
Share of contacts that pass verification: [use 80% if I don't know]
Companies that fit, if I know it: [number or "unknown"]

Do this:
1) Write my fit rules and a no list in a short table.
2) Calculate people to reach, raw contacts and companies needed per month. Round up.
3) If I gave a company count, calculate my runway in months. If it is under 3 months, suggest 3 ways to widen the crowd without losing fit.
4) Split the crowd into 4 to 8 segments and give each one a name, a likely problem and one first-line idea.
5) Tell me how many people must finish the sequence before I judge each angle.
Show everything in tables. No hype.

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: 28 people, 1 reply. If you want more replies, you mostly need more right-fit people, not a cleverer email.

faq.q: Isn't "1 in 28" just a reply rate?
faq.a: It is, but counted per person, not per email. Many sending tools count replies per email sent, and a sequence sends several emails to each person. When you size your crowd, plan in people, because people are what you run out of.

faq.q: What if my whole market is only a few hundred companies?
faq.a: Then go deep, not wide. Make every email very personal, add a second buyer role at each company only if the first one doesn't answer, and use other channels too. Hunter found **50.5% of decision makers** now prefer LinkedIn for outreach.

faq.q: How big should each segment be?
faq.a: Send in groups of about 50 people who share an industry, role and problem, like Hunter's best-performing range. But judge each angle on the total across its groups, a few hundred people, not on one group of 50.

faq.q: Can I just buy a bigger list?
faq.a: Only if it fits your rules and passes verification. A bigger list of the wrong people adds bounces and "not interested" replies, not sales. Count right-fit people, not rows in a spreadsheet.
